prompt.context: Power Gas Retail is a gasoline retailing company and is a big player in the US. They have invested significantly in brand building in the past to differentiate themselves from other competitors. A new CMO has joined the company and wants to know if this brand building exercise makes sense and if it is worth pursuing. You are his consultant and have only 4 weeks to present your findings.
prompt.question: How would you go about evaluating whether the brand building investment makes sense and is worth pursuing?

clarifying_info.q: What types of gasoline does the company sell?
How many retail outlets does the company operate?
clarifying_info.a: Approximately 5,000 gas stations across the country.

clarifying_info.q: How are we defining brand building — is this a one-time campaign or ongoing?
clarifying_info.a: The investment in branding is continual and not limited to occasional campaigns.

clarifying_info.q: What data do we have available?
clarifying_info.a: A consumer survey was conducted over 1 month at 1 retail gas station. Charts showing percentage of customers who fill gas at the station for various reasons are available for both regular and premium unleaded.

clarifying_info.q: What are the monthly sales volumes at a typical outlet?
clarifying_info.a: Total monthly gasoline sales at the outlet are 200,000 gallons — 60% regular unleaded and 40% premium unleaded.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average branding spend?
clarifying_info.a: Average spending on branding is 2 cents per gallon.

clarifying_info.q: What are the margins per gallon?
clarifying_info.a: Margin on one gallon of regular is 5 cents; margin on one gallon of premium is 7 cents.

exhibits.title: Regular Unleaded — Reasons Customers Fill Gas at the Station
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing the percentage breakdown of reasons why customers choose this station for regular unleaded gasoline.

exhibits.title: Premium Unleaded — Reasons Customers Fill Gas at the Station
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing the percentage breakdown of reasons why customers choose this station for premium unleaded gasoline.

framework: Measure branding effectiveness: identify how to attribute sales to the branding investment

Approach options: (a) run a test campaign and track incremental sales; (b) mine historical data and model advertisement elasticity of demand; (c) measure brand recall; (d) conduct a consumer survey to determine what share of customers are driven by brand perception
Selected approach: consumer survey at one retail outlet to measure percentage of revenues attributable to brand perception
Quantify the financial impact: calculate incremental margin from brand-driven customers vs. total branding cost
Scale findings to the full network and assess total profitability
Identify risks and limitations of the methodology

questions.prompt: Walk through the consumer survey approach. What share of customers at the survey outlet buy because of brand perception?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2. For regular unleaded, 35% of customers cite brand perception. For premium unleaded, 50% of customers cite brand perception. Candidate should note that the percentage of customers is assumed to be a fair representation of revenues.

questions.prompt: Calculate the monthly net profit from branding at this one retail outlet.
questions.guidance: Candidate should work through regular and premium separately, then sum. Key inputs: 200,000 total gallons, 60/40 split, 35%/50% brand-driven, margins of 0.10/0.15 per gallon (excluding branding), branding cost of $0.02 per gallon. The net profit per outlet per month is $6,200.

math.setup: Total gallons = 200,000. Regular = 200,000 × 60% = 120,000 gal; Premium = 200,000 × 40% = 80,000 gal. Brand-driven gallons: Regular = 120,000 × 35% = 42,000; Premium = 80,000 × 50% = 40,000. Margin contribution from branding: Regular = 42,000 × $0.10 = $4,200; Premium = 40,000 × $0.15 = $6,000. Branding cost: Total gallons × $0.02 = Regular share = 120,000 × $0.02 = $2,400; Premium share = 80,000 × $0.02 = $1,600. Net monthly profit: Regular = $4,200 − $2,400 = $1,800; Premium = $6,000 − $1,600 = $4,400.
steps: Total net monthly profit per outlet: $1,800 + $4,400 = $6,200
math.answer: $6,200 net monthly profit per retail outlet

questions.prompt: Scale the analysis to the full network of 5,000 stations. What is the annual profit from branding?
questions.guidance: Multiply the per-outlet monthly profit by 5,000 outlets and 12 months.

math.setup: Annual profit = per-outlet monthly profit × 5,000 outlets × 12 months

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential risks with this approach to determining branding effectiveness?

categories.name: Sampling and representativeness
ideas: The study is based on a single retail station and may not be representative of all retail outlets across different geographies and demographics
One month of data may not capture seasonal variation in customer behavior

categories.name: Survey methodology
ideas: A customer may have multiple overlapping reasons for choosing a station, not just one primary reason — the single-reason attribution may overstate brand impact
Self-reported survey data may not accurately reflect actual purchase drivers (social desirability bias)

categories.name: Opportunity cost and relative ROI
ideas: Though branding appears profitable in absolute terms, the ROI may be lower than alternative investments (e.g., store improvements, loyalty programs, price promotions)
The analysis does not assess whether the same spend deployed differently could generate greater returns

recommendation: Investment in branding is a profitable proposition: the company generates approximately $372 million in annual net profit attributable to branding across its 5,000-station network

The return on branding spend is notably higher for premium unleaded ($4,400/month net vs. $1,800/month for regular), suggesting the CMO should consider directing proportionally more brand investment toward premium-tier customers
risks: Study is based on one retail station and may not be nationally representative
Survey methodology assumes a single reason per customer; actual purchase decisions may be multi-factor
Absolute profitability is positive, but ROI relative to alternative initiatives has not been benchmarked
next_steps: Expand the consumer survey to a statistically representative sample of outlets across regions
Conduct sensitivity analysis on margin assumptions and branding spend levels
Benchmark branding ROI against other potential marketing and operational investments
